These results were used to help understand opportunities and tradeoffs for fuel selection based on trip characteristics and rail fuel demand centers. They can also be used in the future to help screen for potential environmental health and 45 safety hotspots. This analysis combined a review of rail routing, commodity movements, and potential fueling locations to identify potential early adopters and initial fuel distribution. Section 5.2 focuses on understanding fuel consumption, and route characteristics to develop strategies for the implementation of alternative fuels in the rail industry. 5.2.1 Datasets for Regional Freight Rail Energy Use and Corridor Identification This analysis uses data from three primary sources: FAF (USDOT, 2017), CWS (STB, 2025), and EIA’s Distillate Fuel Oil Sales Dataset (EIA, 2025). FAF (USDOT, 2025) contains crucial data on the U.S. freight rail system. It is a shipper-based dataset that provides information on the origin and destination of goods from the shipper’s perspective, but it does not specify the exact routes taken. Similarly, CWS (STB, 2025) gives a comprehensive picture of the freight rail activity. It is a carrier-based dataset that offers a more detailed view of rail carriers and routes. However, CWS has confidentiality restrictions to protect commercial interests. It is available in two versions: • The Public Use Waybill Sample (PUWS) provides origin-destination (OD) movements only at the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) level, with around half of the tonnages suppressed to protect confidentiality. • The Confidential Carload Waybill Sample (CCWS) offers more granular information, including individual movements at the county level with railroads and interchange locations, but it cannot be directly used due to confidentiality concerns. However, the CCWS has been valuable for validating the county-level OD movements. The Distillate Fuel Oil Sales Dataset (EIA 2025) offers annual data on the sale and distribution of distillate fuel oil by state. The data is available up to the year 2020. Apart from OD movements, this analysis also relies on the rail freight network data. The NARN published by the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, provides a detailed geographic representation of the railway infrastructure across North America. 5.2.2 Data Limitations and Methodology for the Freight Rail Analysis While FAF (USDOT, 2017) provides a shipper-based outlook on commodity movements between origin and destination, the intermediate stops or transfer locations are unknown. With the addition of PUWS (STB, 2025), a carrier-based movement, a single OD record from FAF could be broken down to multiple records but only at an aggregated level. Hence, to address the limitations in both datasets, a combined dataset was created. This dataset merged county-level OD movements from FAF with BEA-level data from PUWS. Specifically, BEA-level marginal totals were sourced from PUWS only in instances where total flows between BEA regions exceeded FAF totals. For flows where FAF totals were higher, it was assumed that PUWS flows were suppressed and therefore not updated in combined dataset.
